title: 35-year-old took on $20K in debt to launch a business from her dining room—now it brings in 8 figures a year
description: Set Active CEO Lindsey Carter used to lose sleep, cry to her friends and struggle to be present in her personal life after a rough day at work.It's no
body: Set Active CEO Lindsey Carter used to lose sleep, cry to her friends and struggle to be present in her personal life after a rough day at work.It's not that she expected entrepreneurship to be easy. Carter took on $20,000 in personal credit card debt and filled her Los Angeles home with inventory when she started the athleisure company in May 2018, she says. Yet years of obstacles — familiar to many an entrepreneur — followed as she tried to break Set Active into a crowded activewear industry. It took her time to figure out how to separate her professional stress from her personal life."I started understanding that struggle wasn't necessarily a sign that something was going wrong. Sometimes it's just the reality of building something ambitious," says Carter, 35. "And if I was going to let every setback rob me of my happiness, I'm going to be spending a very long time being unhappy."Set Active is no industry giant, but it brought in eight figures in 2025 net sales and is profitable, according to documents reviewed by CNBC Make It. That comes as growth in the broader activewear market has slowed: Women's activewear spending in the U.S. increased 2% between October 2025 and September 2026, down from 7% over the preceding 12 months, according to data from market research firm Circana.Activewear still makes up 30% of U.S. apparel spending, says Circana apparel industry analyst Kristen Classi-Zummo. Shoppers these days particularly gravitate toward casual outfits and loungewear, like sweatpants and sweatshirts, over more active items like leggings and sports bras, Classi-Zummo says. That's good news for Carter, who sells color- and pattern-filled clothing sets that aren't solely intended for workouts. Set Active's Instagram posts feature women sitting on pickleball courts or the banks of the Seine in Paris.Before launching Set Active, Carter ran her own social media company. While shopping around Los Angeles, she struggled to find matching sets of workout clothes she could wear while running errands, meeting a friend for coffee or working from home. "Everything was like yoga poses and upside-down headstands, and I was just like, 'That's not me,'" she says.Her business idea became more real when an associate connected her with a production professional, she says. She decided to order some samples, collected feedback from friends and drew directly on the products with a permanent marker at her dining room table before sending them back to the manufacturer's designers, she says.Going into debt to officially launch the business was just the first among many obstacles while growing Set Active. Some were personal: Carter had two children after starting the company and has never taken maternity leave. She now calls that decision "probably one of the biggest mistakes I've ever made."She experienced what she describes as symptoms of postpartum depression in 2023, and felt like "a horrible version of myself" while simultaneously running the startup. "I let people down. I let friends down. I let employees down and I just wasn't my best self."Other challenges have been professional. In 2026, Set Active has struggled to consistently deliver orders to customers on time, says Carter. The reasons are varied, she says, declining to go into detail, and the stakes are high approaching the holiday shopping season.On Oct. 19, Carter wrote on Instagram that Set Active would cancel its Black Friday and Cyber Monday product launches until further notice. The company won't "drop" any clothes until the products arrive in the company's Los Angeles warehouse, putting a projected $10-plus million in sales during the most popular shopping days of the year at risk, she wrote."I'm walking away from a hefty revenue number," Carter now says, adding: "But at the end of the day, I built this brand on transparency and community, and the customer comes first to me always. And I'd rather make it right with the customer than hit a revenue goal."A hard workday can still make her toss and turn at night, but she's learned how to return home to her family feeling grateful, she says. She gets satisfaction from solving problems and doing a job she believes in, she adds."I just take things day by day with the mindset that challenges are opportunities, and I don't really see them as the enemy," says Carter. "I think that when you sign up to be an entrepreneur, you're signing up for what that journey is going to bring."

title: Qatari mediators held talks in Tehran aimed at restarting direct U.S.-Iran negotiations, source says
description: An AI-based anti-U.S. animation depicting Lego-shaped images of the Chinese Dragon, the legendary Persian Simurgh, and the Statue of Liberty is displa
body: An AI-based anti-U.S. animation depicting Lego-shaped images of the Chinese Dragon, the legendary Persian Simurgh, and the Statue of Liberty is displayed during the 2nd Media-Expo International Exhibition in Tehran, Iran, on October 29, 2026. (Photo by Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto via Getty Images)Nurphoto | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesQatari mediators have held talks with Iranian officials in an attempt to restart direct negotiations between Washington and Tehran, an official source familiar with the discussions told CNBC on Saturday.Iran promised a "geographically unrestricted response" to any new attacks by the U.S.Qatari mediators held more than 12 hours of talks in Tehran on Friday to reach a deal to avoid a possible resumption of American-led attacks on Iran after the U.S. midterm elections, the source said, speaking on condition of anonymity. Axios first reported the talks, which it said are set to continue in the Qatari capital, Doha, on Saturday.Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said there are no plans to meet U.S. officials, adding that an Iranian delegation has headed to Qatar for talks with mediators, Qatari media outlet Al Jazeera reported."What is being circulated in this regard is merely media speculation," Al Jazeera quoted Araghchi as saying.A preliminary agreement signed on June 17 between the U.S. and Iran to halt the fighting — which began on Feb. 28 with U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iranian targets — broke down weeks later.On Tuesday, U.S. President Donald Trump reiterated his claim that the Iran war will end "whenever I want it to." Trump said it "would be very quick, but we have to have an end properly," with a "total statement" that Iran would never have a nuclear weapon.The last confirmed U.S. strikes on Iran occurred on Sept. 1. Trump previously left open the possibility that attacks on Iran would resume after the Nov. 3 midterm elections, which are set for Tuesday. Tehran has said it is preparing a military response to any U.S. strikes.A statement posted on Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei's Telegram account Saturday said that "any level or type of threat must be met with an immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response."Shipping attacks continueThe Iranian Broadcasting Agency quoted a Hormozgan province official as saying Saturday that U.S. forces attacked two fishing boats off Masan near Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz. The report has not been independently confirmed.U.S. Central Command did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.It's the latest report of attacks on shipping in the economically crucial stretch of water.The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre reported Friday that a crude oil tanker was hit by an unknown projectile as it was heading out of the strait.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconBrent crude oil price, U.S. dollars per barrel, year to dateSeparately, Iran said Friday four tankers struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz and Yemen's Houthis claimed missile strikes on Saudi Arabia, escalating pressure on two fronts.The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said three tankers caught fire after striking mines along what it called an "unauthorized southern route" near the Omani coast. Iran's army said a fourth burned east of the strait.Oil prices jumped more than 2% on Friday and settled ​at their highest levels since the end of April, as traders braced for a potential escalation in the war.Brent crude futures for December, which expired on Friday, settled up $2.76, or 2.4%, at $117.64 a barrel, after touching a high of $118. The more active January contract gained $2.63 to $113.43.

title: Binance loses $6.3 billion in crypto heist—what happens to your money when an exchange gets hacked
description: A record-breaking hack at Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, is a reminder of the risks investors take when trusting a company to h
body: A record-breaking hack at Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, is a reminder of the risks investors take when trusting a company to hold their digital tokens.  Binance said Friday that the security breach affected about $6.3 billion in client assets, making it the largest crypto hack on record. Around $3 billion of the affected assets has been frozen on blockchain networks, and the exchange says it has begun recovering some of them.Binance's initial investigation suggests hackers gained access to the firm's withdrawal systems and were able to make unauthorized transfers from the exchange's crypto wallets, according to the company. The company says it has found no evidence that the private keys controlling those wallets were leaked and is still investigating the full scope of the breach.The company says it will cover customers' losses. Binance maintains a roughly $1 billion emergency fund known as SAFU, which was created to protect customers in the event of a security breach. The company initially said SAFU and company funds would cover the losses, and has since said it has set aside more than $6.3 billion of its own funds.For crypto investors, the Binance breach highlights one of the risks of keeping assets on an exchange. While exchanges make it easier to buy, sell and store crypto, what happens after a hack can vary widely, including whether customers get their money back. What happens to your crypto when an exchange gets hackedCrypto exchange hacks aren't uncommon. Hackers stole roughly $1.5 billion from Dubai-based exchange Bybit in 2025, while Seychelles-registered Bitget lost more than $387 million in a hack in September 2026.But a hack doesn't necessarily mean customers will lose their money permanently. Stolen assets can sometimes be recovered or frozen — preventing the hackers from moving or cashing them out — and exchanges may also have insurance, dedicated emergency funds or other company resources available to cover losses. In Binance's case, roughly half of the affected assets have already been frozen, preventing some of the stolen crypto from being moved. Its roughly $1 billion SAFU emergency reserve provides another backstop, if needed.Customers don't always recover stolen digital assets quickly. New Zealand exchange Cryptopia was forced into liquidation months after a 2019 hack in which about NZ$30 million in crypto was stolen. The liquidation process stretched on for years, with the first distributions finally beginning in 2024. "When you leave crypto on an exchange, you are relying on that company's controls and its balance sheet," says Martin Mulyadi, YHB Endowed Chair in Accounting and professor of accounting at Shenandoah University. "A pledge to make customers whole is only as strong as the resources behind it."What you should look for when choosing a crypto exchangeWhen considering where to transact in and hold crypto, start by researching the exchange itself. The Securities and Exchange Commission recommends searching for customer complaints and checking how the exchange is regulated. U.S. customers can also check whether an exchange is registered with the Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, or FinCEN, using its online database. Registration can help confirm that you're dealing with an identifiable business operating within the U.S. regulatory system, though FinCEN cautions that registration isn't an endorsement of the company. Crypto experts also recommend reading an exchange's user agreement or terms of service. Some exchanges might have separate custody agreements or risk disclosures that are worth checking, too, Mulyadi says.Look for language explaining who owns your crypto and what the exchange can do with it. Phrases such as "you retain title" or assets being "held for your benefit" are good signs, Mulyadi says. Check whether customer assets are kept separate from the exchange's own, which can offer extra protection if the company fails. And find out whether the exchange can lend or otherwise use your crypto, which can expose your assets to additional risk.In the user agreement, check the exchange's limitation-of-liability section, Mulyadi says, and look at what insurance coverage the exchange offers and what it actually covers. "If a refund after a hack is at the exchange's discretion, it's a goodwill gesture, not a promise," Mulyadi says.Even strong language in the terms isn't a guarantee that your assets will be safe. FTX, the popular crypto exchange that collapsed in 2022, misappropriated billions of dollars in customer funds even though its terms said those assets belonged to customers, Mulyadi says.Is it safer to keep your crypto on an exchange or hold it yourself?If you don't want to hold your crypto through an exchange, there's another option known as "self-custody."With self-custody, you use your own crypto wallet and control the private keys used to authorize transactions on the blockchain. Wallets typically come with a recovery phrase — essentially a master password that can be used to restore access to the wallet if you lose it.That gives you control of your crypto without relying on an exchange, but it also makes you responsible for keeping that information safe.And for anyone who's ever lost or forgotten a password, the risks of self-custody are real. With self-custody, there is "no help desk if you lose your recovery phrase," Mulyadi says.For many investors, Mulyadi says a middle ground is keeping only what they actively trade on an exchange and holding longer-term assets themselves, as long as they understand how to safely store and recover them."Coins on an exchange are a promise from a company; coins in your own wallet are a responsibility you can't hand off," Mulyadi says.

title: SpaceX loses bid to toss NAACP lawsuit over Memphis data center air pollution
description: SpaceX is building a massive gas turbine power plant in Southaven, Mississippi to power its data centers in the area.SpaceX's AI division, SpaceXAI, l
body: SpaceX is building a massive gas turbine power plant in Southaven, Mississippi to power its data centers in the area.SpaceX's AI division, SpaceXAI, lost its bid to dismiss an NAACP lawsuit, which is proceeding in federal court in Mississippi, according to a judge's opinion released late Friday. The lawsuit claims that the AI division of CEO Elon Musk's aerospace and defense tech conglomerate violated the Clean Air Act with its use of gas-fired combustion turbines to power its massive AI data centers in Greater Memphis. The Colossus data centers and a power plant that SpaceXAI is also building in Southaven, Mississippi, have faced community backlash for years.The Southern Environmental Law Center and Earthjustice filed the suit on behalf of the NAACP in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Mississippi in April 2026. The suit alleges that between August and December 2025, xAI and its subsidiary MZX Tech, installed and operated 27 gas turbines in Southaven, Mississippi, "without an air permit or regard for the health and safety of people living nearby." (SpaceXAI is owned and operated by SpaceX, which has rebranded it as SpaceXAI or SpaceXSI.)The turbines emit smog-forming pollutants and particulate matter that can increase health risks and cause an unpleasant odor, among other unwanted impacts, according to the suit. Lawyers for SpaceXAI argued in their motion to dismiss, filed in June, that the NAACP suit should be tossed because the company's use of the turbines, which it characterized as "mobile," was exempt from permitting requirements. They also argued that NAACP didn't have a right to sue under the federal Clean Air Act, and suits by such community groups were unconstitutional.The judge presiding over the case rejected those arguments, writing: "Because the plaintiffs have statutory standing under the Clean Air Act, because the combustion turbines are not 'mobile sources' under Mississippi's SIP, and because the citizen suit provision does not violate Article II of the Constitution or the private nondelegation doctrine, the plaintiffs' claims will proceed."The decision comes about two weeks after the same court rejected a Department of Justice's request to end the case against Musk's company. SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment.watch now

title: OpenAI pares fundraising goal, now seeking up to $20 billion in latest round
description: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman speaking at Oracle AI World in Las Vegas, Nevada, on Oct. 27, 2026.CNBCOpenAI is seeking to raise up to $20 billion in a new fun
body: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman speaking at Oracle AI World in Las Vegas, Nevada, on Oct. 27, 2026.CNBCOpenAI is seeking to raise up to $20 billion in a new funding round, CNBC confirmed on Saturday, paring back its earlier target of up to $30 billion.The funding round is still in progress and has not closed, so the figures are subject to change, a person directly familiar with the deal told CNBC, asking to remain unnamed as they were not authorized to discuss the details publicly.OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.The Financial Times first reported that OpenAI had reduced its target for the round by $10 billion, and said the company would seek a post-money valuation of $1.25 trillion. According to FT, the ChatGPT developer set a Friday deadline for investors to commit to ​the newest round, with some investors opting to reduce their allocations.Investors from the United Arab Emirates are leading the round alongside Coatue, as CNBC previously reported.News that the ChatGPT developer slashed its funding round follows a week when investors asked whether big tech firms' spending on AI, especially to build out data centers and snap up GPUs, will deliver adequate returns.AI-linked stocks sank on Friday, with chip maker Intel down 25% on lackluster revenue guidance, Micron down 5.5%, and Nvidia falling 4%. Microsoft, Alphabet's Google and Amazon have been on a spending blitz in recent years to meet the surge in demand for AI infrastructure, but all three issued capex figures or forecasts last week that came in below analysts' estimates. Alphabet saw its worst trading day ever on Thursday after its search revenue fell short of expectations. Philipp Schindler, the company's chief business officer, said the impact on search was partly because of lower monetization within the company's AI Mode.watch now

title: In the wake of Weil, a legal recruiter's advice for surviving a company wind-down
description: It's hard to believe a corporate giant like Weil, Gotshal & Manges — a top 20 U.S. law firm that reportedly had over $2 billion in revenue in 2025 — c
body: It's hard to believe a corporate giant like Weil, Gotshal & Manges — a top 20 U.S. law firm that reportedly had over $2 billion in revenue in 2025 — could move toward ceasing operations just like that. But occasionally a Weil-like wind-down — or even a collapse like Lehman Brothers, Silicon Valley Bank or FTX — is bound to occur. And here we are, seeing a major law firm move toward shutting down in real time. The firm's management committee recommended that its partners prepare to close its doors after more than 90 years in business, Weil, Gotshal & Manges said on Wednesday. "Following a careful review of strategic alternatives, the Firm's Management Committee has recommended to the partnership that the Firm pursue an orderly wind-down," the firm said in a statement to CNBC on Wednesday. "The partners are expected to vote in the coming days."As a legal recruiter and former big law associate, I'm here to provide practical insights to the employees, lawyers and non-lawyers alike, who've just learned they're about to be out of a job — and those who are scared their company might be next. First, let's be clear: From where I stand, Weil is an anomaly. But when a company does make headlines for winding down, or failing and shutting down, it's rarely the employees whose plight is highlighted: the people whose careers have been destabilized, whose anxiety shoots through the roof and who become the collateral damage of business decisions they had no idea were being made until far too late. Here are my top tips, for both lawyers and non-lawyers, for when your company announces or is headed toward dissolution. In the case of Weil, it's advice I hope the firm's roughly 1,200 lawyers plus staff take to heart in the next 90 days. 1. Don't wait for the dust to settle Yes, you can worry. Yes, you can grieve. But you should also mobilize quickly.A lot of Weil associates are in a holding pattern right now: either waiting to see where their favorite partners are going and hoping they offer to bring them along, or thinking 90 days of pay, as reported by Reuters, means they have 90 days in which to start looking.While many associates will eventually follow their partners, I suggest looking for a new job on your own while you wait. The market is absolutely inundated with Weil associates right now, on top of everyone else whose firm isn't dissolving but was already looking to make a lateral move. You don't want to be late to the party and find all your peers are ahead of you in line. Partners are also under no obligation to bring you with them, and you have no say in where they choose to go. There's no guarantee it would be a good fit for you. It's best to have options and it's comforting to feel like you have some control over those options, especially in such uncertain times. I'd give similar advice to non-lawyers. Don't wait too long. Options are always good. Be proactive. The people who tend to come out of these situations the least scathed are the ones who start looking before any announcement is made, in cases where the writing's on the wall and everyone else is still hoping for a last-minute save.2. Don't act from a place of fearEven as you move fast, try to be cautious. You don't want to be taken advantage of. Just this week, I've counseled about a dozen Weil associates to do their homework, however quickly, before blasting their resume to every firm and recruiter on the block. Some recruiters — especially in the legal industry — will take you sending your resume as blanket consent to submit you anywhere they like. But from what I've seen working in legal recruiting, if more than one recruiter sends your materials to the same firm, you're very unlikely to ever hear from that firm again. They see it as sloppy, bad form and too much of a headache to manage the inevitable fight over who's entitled to the hypothetical fee for your placement. So keep a firm grasp on where your resume is at all times. You should know exactly which companies have it and who they got it from. If you plan to use a recruiter, pick a reputable and trusted one. Don't race to the first recruiter who cold calls you or the last recruiter in your inbox. Instead, get referrals from friends, set up intro calls with multiple recruiters to get a vibe check, pick one and only send that one your resume.For non-legal folks, recruiting may not be so cutthroat. But I still recommend caution regarding how and where you share your information. Focus on trusted connections, including verifiable HR professionals at your target companies, friend and colleague referrals, your college career services office and known job boards. Be wary of answering outreach from questionable sources.  3. Don't worry so much about resume gaps or job hops right nowA short unemployment stint won't kill your career, and neither will multiple moves in quick succession. When the unexpected occurs and the resulting job market frenzy ensues, sometimes, even when you mobilize early and wisely, you won't land a new job right away. Perhaps the only upside to the mass publicity of these surprise dissolutions is that every prospective employer is going to take one look at your resume and understand why you're out of work. They won't wonder what you did wrong, whether you got fired or if you're qualified. But those favorable assumptions don't last forever. I'd give it one to six months. That's another plug for not waiting until a dissolution date to start your search, especially in the current job market, where as of September 27.1% of those who are unemployed have been searching for over six months, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Keep in mind too that job decisions made in haste or with your back against a wall are much more likely to end in a mismatch. Most people will take the first offer they get. Some will accept an unsustainable commute or a tyrant of a boss for short-term job security. And if it's your only option, that might be the right decision for you — we all have bills to pay and mouths to feed. If that's the case, know it's also okay to move on quickly. I don't begrudge anyone who makes a job decision out of necessity and then course corrects when they're out of survival mode. And from my experience as a recruiter, neither will most future employers. 4. Be kind to yourself and others None of this is your fault and all of it is horribly unfair. It's okay if you're feeling angry, terrified, overwhelmed, frozen, devastated or even a little relieved. Whatever you're feeling, both in the immediate aftermath and in the weeks and months after, is completely valid. Give yourself ample space and grace for whatever comes up and seek help and support.  On the flip side, lend a helping hand wherever you can, especially once you find a job, which I believe you will. Pay it forward by helping others who are still looking or looking again. Share a good resource, refer them to a trusted recruiter and connect them to any job opportunities you've passed up or heard about. Corporations don't have feelings or loyalty to any given employee. But people do. We are nothing without our empathy and our communities. Hard times are when we need both the most. Danielle Thompson is a legal recruiter and former big law employment lawyer based in the Bay Area. A managing director at Damato Search Group, she holds a J.D. from Columbia Law School and a B.A., magna cum laude, from UC Santa Barbara.

schema.headline: In the wake of Weil, a legal recruiter's advice for surviving a company wind-down

title: Anthropic's path to the Nasdaq just got a lot bumpier
description: Co-founder and CEO of Anthropic Dario Amodei looks on as President Donald Trump speaks to the press after a meeting with technology executives about a
body: Co-founder and CEO of Anthropic Dario Amodei looks on as President Donald Trump speaks to the press after a meeting with technology executives about artificial intelligence at the White House in Washington, Sept. 29, 2026.Kent Nishimura | AFP | Getty ImagesAnthropic picked a tough week to unveil its IPO prospectus. Within days of its release, several of the company's key partners, including Microsoft, Google and Amazon, reported quarterly results that added fuel to existing market jitters around the artificial intelligence buildout. "Everybody's still full steam ahead on AI, but all the things around it took an interesting turn this week," Daniel Newman, CEO at Futurum Group, told CNBC in an interview on Friday. The hyperscalers' results have "raised eyebrows" and created a new headwind in the market, which is "more doubt on capital structure," he said. No matter the current state of the market, Anthropic was going to have to address a skeptical investor base as it pursues a potentially record-setting initial public offering in the coming weeks. In its prospectus on Monday, the AI company disclosed a net loss for the first half of the year of $80 billion, alongside hundreds of billions of dollars' worth of compute commitments and more than 90 pages of risk factors. Investors are still waiting to see Anthropic's third-quarter financials. Heading into this week, fears were mounting about the financial health of neoclouds like CoreWeave and Nebius, which are facing rising borrowing costs and a dearth of lenders as they pursue aggressive AI buildouts. Anthropic gets much of its capacity from Amazon, Google and SpaceX, but it also relies on neoclouds for some compute as it races to expand as quickly as possible. Now investors are growing increasingly worried about the whole AI trade.  "It's a great technology, seems to do things that we never would have imagined, but how does that then translate into a viable business?" David Hsu, a professor at the University of Pennsylvania Wharton School, said in an interview.The Nasdaq Composite notched its first three-week losing streak since March after plunging 2.9% on Friday. Nvidia, whose graphics processing units have powered the AI boom, traded lower, along with the whole semiconductor sector, after Intel issued a weak forecast, sending its stock to its steepest drop since the 1970s. Microsoft, Google and Amazon all had notes of concern this week in their reports. The companies have been on a spending blitz in recent years to meet the surge in demand for AI infrastructure, but all three issued capex figures or forecasts that came in below analysts' estimates. Microsoft lowered its capex forecast for the year to $170 billion from $175 billion, while Alphabet maintained its guidance for up to $205 billion and Amazon reiterated its roughly $220 billion forecast."It's been an ugly reporting season for tech thus far," Jonathan Krinsky, managing director at BTIG, wrote in a Thursday note. He described the fallout as "The Techsas Chainsaw Massacre," adding that there's too much weakness in the sector for the market to ignore. Cash is becoming an issue. Amazon reported negative free cash flow for the second consecutive quarter, recording an outflow of $42.4 billion for the trailing 12-month period. Google reported negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion, one reason the stock tanked almost 13% on Thursday, its worst day ever. Microsoft maintained positive free cash flow of $18.6 billion, but it's down significantly for a second straight quarter. The company announced plans on Thursday to raise $25 billion in bonds, as it seeks additional sources of funding to help finance its infrastructure expansion. "Suddenly, they're like, 'We can't keep funding this on free cash flow,'" Newman said. "The worry is that basically now there's no company that's able to do this using their own business capabilities to create cash flow. It's becoming increasingly alarming."Cloud growth remains strongAnthropic's hyperscaler partners are also among its biggest investors. The companies all need each other to keep the flywheel turning, a topic that's sure to be a major point of discussion in Anthropic's upcoming roadshow. Anthropic didn't immediately respond to a request for comment. A big tail wind for Anthropic remains AI demand. Microsoft, Google and Amazon all reported cloud growth that topped analysts' estimates, with revenue in Google's business more than doubling from a year earlier. And Oracle, one of the biggest spenders on AI data centers, said at its investor day on Wednesday that it will limit additional fundraising in the coming years to $20 billion, and will turn cash flow positive in the second half of next fiscal year. Analysts at Citizens wrote in a Thursday report that the announcement "put the biggest investor fear to rest — that funding its enormous AI infrastructure buildout would require an open-ended increase in debt and equity issuance."watch nowAttention will now turn back from hyperscaler earnings to Anthropic, as investors assess how much risk they're willing to assume and at what price. The IPO market has largely been frozen since SpaceX's record offering in June. Biometric ring maker Oura, Australian AI data center operator Firmus and SK Hynix's U.S.-based Solidigm subsidiary have all recently postponed or abandoned plans to IPO. Nscale, a neocloud that filed to go public in September, hasn't updated its prospectus in weeks, nor has SoftBank's SB Energy. With Anthropic, Newman said the FOMO — fear of missing out — on a potentially "generational" company is real, and that the prospectus was "very impressive," showing 1,300% annual sales growth, 900% net revenue retention and an implied gross margin of 85%.  "Anthropic is the IPO market at this point," Newman said. "I think companies would have to be extremely cautious, if not just foolish, to actually want to come out in this period."— CNBC's Jordan Novet, Annie Palmer and Samantha Subin contributed to this report.WATCH: Anthropic’s heavy AI spending could hold the key to its profitability: Ark Investwatch now

title: Treasury Department announces new Series I bond rate of 5.51% for the next six months
description: Jetcityimage | Istock | Getty ImagesThe U.S. Department of the Treasury has announced new rates for Series I bonds. Newly purchased I bonds will pay 5
body: Jetcityimage | Istock | Getty ImagesThe U.S. Department of the Treasury has announced new rates for Series I bonds. Newly purchased I bonds will pay 5.51% annual interest from Nov. 1 through April 30, which is up from the 4.26% yield offered on purchases made through Oct. 31.The new rate includes a variable portion of 4.08% based on inflation data, and a fixed portion of 1.40%. The fixed rate is up from 0.90% announced in April, and the highest since 2006. Combined, the composite I bond rate is 5.51% after rounding, according to the Treasury. Read more CNBC personal finance coverageIf Elon Musk gifts SpaceX stock through Trump Accounts, it will come with a catchRoth conversions aren't for everyone. When the 'juice' isn't worth it: Top advisorThe affordability crisis isn't hitting all voters equally. Here's whyMidterm elections: How affordability and the economy could affect voters' decisionsCNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 rankedCNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026Amid the post-pandemic inflation peak, the I bond rate hit a record high of 9.62% in May 2022, and investors poured millions into the government-backed, nearly risk-free asset. As inflation cooled and I bond rates fell, many short-term investors redeemed I bonds. But investors could return as inflation pushes I bond rates back up, experts say. "I bonds are a lot more attractive at this point," said David Enna, founder of Tipswatch.com, a website that tracks Treasury inflation-protected securities, or TIPS, and I bond rates.  I bonds are a lot more attractive at this point.David EnnaFounder of Tipswatch.comThe consumer price index rose 3.7% in September 2026 from one year earlier, up from an annual pace of 3.4% in August, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported in October.In September, some higher inflation came from the Iran war, which pushed up gasoline and energy costs. President Donald Trump's tariffs, new artificial intelligence data centers and demand for travel have also added to rising prices, economists say. Consumers expect rising inflation to continue. In September, the one-year inflation outlook jumped to 3.9%, the highest in more than three years, according to a New York Fed survey released in early October. How I bond rates workI bond rates have a variable and fixed rate portion, which the Treasury adjusts every six months, in May and November. The variable rate is tied to inflation — using the consumer price index percentage change over six months — and stays the same for six months after you purchase, regardless of the Treasury's next update. Your fixed rate doesn't change after purchasing I bonds. The Treasury doesn't disclose how it calculates fixed-rate adjustments, making it harder to predict.Some experts believe the I bond fixed rate could be driven by real, or inflation-adjusted, yields from five-year TIPS, according to Ken Tumin, founder of DepositQuest.com, a blog that tracks I bond rates, among other deposit accounts. "There's some uncertainty there," Tumin said.   How the change affects current I bond investorsIf you currently own I bonds, rate updates follow a six-month timeline based on your original purchase date. After you own I bonds for six months, the variable yield changes to the next announced rate. But the fixed rate stays the same for the entire time you own the asset.For example, let's say you purchased I bonds in March when the variable rate was still 3.12% and the fixed rate was 0.9%. After six months, the variable portion would shift to 3.34%, announced in April 2026, but your fixed rate would remain 0.9%.You can earn I bond interest for up to 30 years, or less if you redeem the assets before that. However, you can't cash in I bonds for at least one year after you buy them. If you redeem within five years, you lose your last three months of interest.

schema.headline: Treasury Department announces new Series I bond rate of 5.51% for the next six months

title: Trump defamation suit against Murdoch, WSJ over Epstein letter dismissed with prejudice
description: U.S. President Donald Trump and Rupert Murdoch. Kevin Lamarque | Ricky Carioti | Via ReutersA federal judge in Miami on Saturday dismissed with prejud
body: U.S. President Donald Trump and Rupert Murdoch. Kevin Lamarque | Ricky Carioti | Via ReutersA federal judge in Miami on Saturday dismissed with prejudice President Donald Trump's amended defamation lawsuit against media baron Rupert Murdoch and The Wall Street Journal over the newspaper's reporting on a purported 50th birthday letter from the president to notorious sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.District Court Judge Darrin Gayles ruled that Trump had again failed to plausibly allege the newspaper and other defendants acted with actual malice when they published the story in July 2025."As with his first attempt, he has failed," Gayles wrote in the 20-page ruling, which came more than six months after he dismissed Trump's first version of the suit. "Grasping at straws, the Amended Complaint attempts to manufacture flaws with the investigation."By dismissing the suit with prejudice, the judge blocked Trump from filing another suit alleging the same claims about Murdoch and the paper in federal court.Gayles said the Journal had conducted a "thoughtful and detailed investigation," and he rejected Trump's argument that the newspaper should not have published the story after he denied writing the letter.The judge did not determine whether Trump actually authored the disputed letter. Trump has adamantly denied writing it.When Galyes first dismissed the suit in April, he allowed Trump to file an amended version of the complaint to cure legal defects the judge had identified.  Trump was seeking $10 billion in damages from Murdoch and the Journal, which is owned by Murdoch's News Corp. A spokesperson for the newspaper's publisher, Dow Jones & Co., in a statement to CNBC on Saturday, said, "We're pleased with the court's decision."A spokesman for Trump's legal team confirmed to CNBC that the president plans to appeal the ruling."President Trump will continue to press forward in his powerhouse lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal and all of the other defendants," the spokesman said in a statement. "The President will continue to hold those who mislead the American People with Fake News and smears accountable for their actions."Gayles, as he did when dismissing the suit for the first time, noted Trump, who has adamantly denied sending the letter to his then-friend Epstein in 2003, had "not plausibly alleged that the Defendants published the Article with actual malice."Plaintiffs who are public figures like Trump must show a defendant acted with actual malice when making allegedly defamatory statements, according to Supreme Court decisions that Gayles cited at the beginning of his ruling.Trump's amended lawsuit contained new details and claims, including that Murdoch told the president "I will handle it" during a phone conversation they had about an article describing a birthday letter to Epstein that allegedly bore Trump's signature, Newsweek previously reported.Gayles rejected each of Trump's arguments in the amended complaint, including that the Journal did not adequately investigate the letter, omitted relevant details, and that the article was published after the president and his representatives denied it was authentic.Gayles said that accepting that last argument would effectively allow public figures to block unfavorable reporting, which "runs afoul of the First Amendment" that protects freedom of speech and the press.Saturday's ruling is the latest setback in litigation between Trump and the media.Another federal judge in Miami on Oct. 22 ordered Trump to sit for a deposition in his $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBC by Dec. 11.A birthday letter that U.S. President Donald Trump allegedly wrote to sex offender Jeffrey Epstein more than 20 years ago is seen as presented by the Democrats in the U.S. House of Representatives on their X account September 8, 2025.Democrats on the House Oversight CommitteeThe Journal's article on July 17, 2025, said a letter bearing Trump's signature was included in an album of letters Epstein was giving for his 50th birthday. The article said Trump sent the letter at the request of Epstein's close friend, Ghislaine Maxwell, who two decades later was convicted of procuring underage girls to be sexually abused by Epstein.The Journal noted that the letter "contains several lines of typewritten text framed by the outline of a naked woman, which appears to be hand-drawn with a heavy marker.""A pair of small arcs denotes the woman's breasts, and the future president's signature is a squiggly 'Donald' below her waist, mimicking pubic hair," Journal reporters Khadeeja Safdar and Joe Palazzolo said in the article."The letter concludes: 'Happy Birthday — and may every day be another wonderful secret,'" they wrote.Trump angrily denied writing the letter, saying, "This is not me. This is a fake thing."'"I never wrote a picture in my life. I don't draw pictures of women," the president said at the time.

title: Meta outlook revised downward by S&P on cash flow and capex concerns
description: CEO of Meta Platforms Mark Zuckerberg attends a press briefing held by U.S. President Donald Trump with AI executives following a meeting on artificia
body: CEO of Meta Platforms Mark Zuckerberg attends a press briefing held by U.S. President Donald Trump with AI executives following a meeting on artificial intelligence, outside the West Wing of the White House on September 29, 2026 in Washington, DC. Finn Gomez | Getty ImagesMeta's outlook has been revised downward by S&P Global Ratings on concerns surrounding cash flow and AI spending.The credit agency said Friday that the outlook reflects "uncertainty" about Meta's elevated capex and its negative free cash flow. Meta's credit rating was revised from AA- stable to AA- negative, S&P said. S&Ps highest credit rating is AAA. Anything below BBB falls into the junk bond category. The agency questioned "Meta's ability to monetize its AI investments" relative to its peers, which are also spending heavily on data center buildouts and going cash flow negative in the process. Although Meta has recently debuted its Muse AI agent app and related foundation models, S&P said "it is unclear when these revenue streams will generate material contributions that exceed their rising costs over the next few years."A Meta spokesperson pushed back on the revision."We respectfully disagree with S&P's assertion about Meta's AI monetization capabilities," the spokesperson said in a statement. "We see significant product and business opportunities ahead of us, supporting our very strong credit profile." Meta said in its third-quarter earnings report last week that it expects full-year capex to come in the range of $135 billion to $145 billion. The company also posted negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion, going in the red for the first time.Investors sent Meta shares down 7% following the report despite a revenue beat. The stock finished October down 15%, its worst month in four years. The company said on Monday that it plans to raise $95 billion to help fund its AI initiatives, with plans to first raise $35 billion in underwritten public equity offerings, followed by an additional $60 billion through an at-the-market program.S&P said that while it expects Meta's capex growth to start "flattening out beginning in 2028," the agency is "less certain that it will curtail its spending as previously anticipated."WATCH: Mike Khouw likes this options strategy for Meta post-earnings.watch now

title: Intel stock has worst day since 1970s, wiping about $12 billion off government's stake
description: Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan speaks during a keynote presentation at Computex in Taipei on June 2, 2026.Cheng Yu-chen | Afp | Getty ImagesIntel shares plummet
body: Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan speaks during a keynote presentation at Computex in Taipei on June 2, 2026.Cheng Yu-chen | Afp | Getty ImagesIntel shares plummeted 29% on Friday, their worst day since the 1970s, after the chipmaker issued weaker-than-expected guidance due to a plant shutdown in Israel and ongoing softness in the PC market. It's a major setback for CEO Lip-Bu Tan, who was hired in March 2025, and has since been on a campaign to revive the company after it missed out on the early years of the artificial intelligence boom. Intel's plunge is also a big hit to the Trump administration, which led the U.S. government into taking a 10% stake in the company over a year ago. While it's still a profitable investment, the value of those holdings dropped by about $12 billion on Friday. Nvidia also took a big stake in Intel, and its stock dropped by about $6 billion in value. Heading into Thursday's earnings report, Intel shares were up about 150% this year, buoyed by demand for central processors, which are becoming critical to agentic AI workloads. Analysts at D.A. Davidson downgraded the stock to neutral from buy on Friday in a report titled, "Not fixed yet.""We understand the PC market is being impacted at the industry level," the analysts wrote. "However it is hard to justify the current multiple when weakness is so significant."Stock Chart IconStock chart iconAmazon and Intel stock chartAmazon shares also sold off on Friday, slipping 1.4%, after the company reported a third-quarter miss on the top and bottom line while maintaining its capital expenditure forecast for 2026 of $220 billion. Amazon also reported negative free cash flow for the second consecutive quarter, and a big increase from the previous period.The Nasdaq Composite slid 2.9%, capping off a week of rough tech earnings. Alphabet on Thursday suffered its worst day on record, plunging more than 12%. The stock fell again on Friday. Other semiconductor names also notched declines. Chip giant Nvidia fell 4%, while Broadcom dropped more than 5% and mobile chipmaker Qualcomm tumbled 11%.Not a 'moment of reckoning'Investors are growing nervous about the massive AI spending from the tech giants and whether their investments will pay off."I don't think this is a moment of reckoning but I think it's a moment where investors should take a long thought about how positioning across the space still remains crowded even though the fundamentals are strong," Matt Orton, chief market strategist at Raymond James, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Friday.For Intel, the disappointing forecast reflects a PC market that's getting hammered due to soaring costs for memory and other components. Global PC shipments declined 4% in the second quarter from a year earlier, according to Counterpoint Research.Read more CNBC tech newsAI build-out hits snag as Google and Microsoft put off raising capex forecastsTrump tech allies swap AI for 'super intelligence' in earnings callsTech giants need legacy businesses to keep growing as they pour trillions into the AI buildoutNvidia responds to accusations that Jensen Huang was Chinese targetIntel said it expects adjusted earnings per share of 25 cents this quarter on revenue between $15 billion and $16 billion. Analysts were expecting revenue of $17.1 billion and EPS of 43 cents, according to LSEG."We see the PC slowdown continuing at least through the first half of next year," Intel finance chief David Zinsner, said in the release. "We will continue making disciplined investments in capacity and working capital to increase supply and support future growth."The guidance also accounts for the effects of an explosion at a fab in Israel that killed two workers and seriously injured a third earlier this month. The incident will cost the company about $600 million in lost revenue over two quarters, Zinsner said. Tan said the explosion, which he called an "unfortunate and tragic accident," caused an "extended shutdown" at the plant, impacting shipments of 10-nanometer chips.Key to Tan's turnaround effort is Intel's foundry business, which has struggled to find its footing.Intel is the only U.S.-based manufacturer of advanced logic chips, and is now in high-volume production of its most advanced 18A chip out of its new fab in Arizona, providing an alternative to Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. Its next Arizona fab is expected to begin operations by the end of 2028.Intel still has no external customers for its new chips."We're going to have a couple of customers ready to announce the next two quarters," Tan said on the call, adding that Intel is making "tremendous progress" on its coming 14A chips.WATCH: KeyBanc keeping its buy rating on Intelwatch now

title: Automatic 401(k) rollovers reduce cash-outs, research finds — but few accounts reach new employer plans
description: Abraham Gonzalez Fernandez | E+ | Getty ImagesLeaving a job can make a small 401(k) hard to hold on to: Some employers' plans cash out accounts under
body: Abraham Gonzalez Fernandez | E+ | Getty ImagesLeaving a job can make a small 401(k) hard to hold on to: Some employers' plans cash out accounts under $1,000 or move slightly larger balances into an IRA. Taking the money in cash and moving on can feel like the simplest option, but it can have short- and long-term financial consequences.A system backed by major 401(k) administrators aims to make it easier for those savings to follow workers to their next job. New research from one of those companies, Vanguard, shows it's helping fewer people cash out — although most of the money has yet to reach workers' new retirement plans.Among workers with less than $1,000 in their 401(k), the share who cashed out within 10 months of leaving their job fell to about 9% from roughly 50% after their employers began participating in a new system called the Portability Services Network, according to the Vanguard research. Among those with balances of between $1,000 and $7,000, the share cashing out fell to 31% from 39%.Portability Services Network is a coalition of large 401(k) administrators — including Vanguard, Fidelity Investments and Alight Solutions, among others — in conjunction with Retirement Clearinghouse and has been in operation since late 2023.Read more CNBC personal finance coverageIf Elon Musk gifts SpaceX stock through Trump Accounts, it will come with a catchRoth conversions aren't for everyone. When the 'juice' isn't worth it: Top advisorThe affordability crisis isn't hitting all voters equally. Here's whyMidterm elections: How affordability and the economy could affect voters' decisionsCNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 rankedCNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026How it works: When a worker with a small 401(k) balance leaves an employer that participates in the network, the money is generally automatically rolled into a safe harbor IRA, where it remains until the network matches it with the worker's new employer plan. The balance then gets rolled into the new 401(k) from that interim IRA. The catch, however, is that the receiving employer must also participate in the network for the money to move to the next employer's plan.In Vanguard's research, just 6% of accounts that have been transferred into IRAs as part of this automatic portability network successfully made it to a new employer's plan as of early 2026, largely because few employers have opted in. The rest generally remained in those interim IRAs, waiting to be matched with another employer plan that participates in the network. While workers can always roll over the money into their new 401(k) themselves, the point of the network is for it to happen automatically.Of the roughly 220,000 outbound rollovers involving Vanguard participants analyzed, the median balance was just $200, and nearly three-quarters involved less than $1,000. The typical saver affected was 31 years old, earned about $20,000 annually and had worked for their employer for roughly six months, according to the research.The cash-out analysis is based on workers at 83 employer-sponsored retirement plans administered by Vanguard that have adopted the automatic portability.Financial consequences of cashing outTypically, when you part ways with an employer, you can leave your money in its 401(k) plan if the account value is above $7,000. Balances under $1,000 usually result in the plan cashing you out and mailing you a check. For amounts between $1,000 and $7,000, most plans roll the balance over to an IRA if the former employee takes no action to move it themselves.Cashing out a 401(k) when leaving a job, whether done by an employer or the employee, can have lasting financial consequences. Workers who withdraw their savings can owe income taxes on the money and may face a 10% early withdrawal penalty if they're younger than 59½. They also lose the opportunity for that money to grow over time.watch nowMost workers — 84% — have changed employers at least once during their careers, while 53% have switched three or more times and 27% have made at least five moves, according to a new study from Empower, a 401(k) recordkeeper and a founding partner of the portability network. The report is based on an online survey of 2,005 adults.Additionally, 50% of Generation Z respondents and 45% of millennials said they may have retirement savings from a previous employer that they've lost track of, the survey found. That compares with 30% of Gen X and 14% of baby boomers.$71.3 million in assets have made it to new plansSince the Portability Services Network's launch in November 2023, there have been 53,118 completed transactions, totaling $71.3 million in assets transferred from a previous employer plan to a new employer plan via automatic portability, according to Steve Holman, senior vice president of Portability Services Network strategy and development at Retirement Clearinghouse.There are 23,787 plans that have adopted automatic portability, representing 7.73 million participants, Holman said. The overall estimate of participants in 401(k)s and similar workplace plans is about 96 million, he said.watch nowThere are 1.22 million eligible participants waiting to be matched with a new employer, up more than 25% since the beginning of 2026, Holman said.Snags remain with the automatic portability processKeeping the money in a safe harbor IRA can be better for investors financially than cashing out — but management fees may take a toll on small balances, especially when the money is in an interest-bearing cash account or other conservative investment."For many of these small accounts, earnings on the conservative default investment may not be sufficient to offset recurring account-level fees while the account remains unmatched, leaving the balance vulnerable to gradual erosion," the Vanguard study said.Workers with Roth savings face another complication. If retirement savings are in a traditional 401(k) — funded with pretax contributions and taxed when withdrawn in retirement — it goes into a traditional IRA. Likewise, Roth 401(k)s, funded with after-tax contributions and withdrawn tax-free down the road, go into Roth IRAs. However, IRS rules don't allow for a Roth IRA to be rolled into a new employer's 401(k), even a Roth 401(k)."We are advocating for future legislation to allow for Roth dollars to be eligible for auto-portability — our technology can support it today," Holman said.

schema.headline: Automatic 401(k) rollovers reduce cash-outs, research finds — but few accounts reach new employer plans

title: Humans are still doing the work behind some AI agents
description: Various examples of avatars for Muse, Meta's AI Agent, during the Meta Connect event in Menlo Park, California, US, on Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026. Minh
body: Various examples of avatars for Muse, Meta's AI Agent, during the Meta Connect event in Menlo Park, California, US, on Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026. Minh Connors | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesThe next time someone's supercharged AI agent attempts to make a phone call to negotiate a cable bill, it could be an actual human who haggles with customer service rather than the software.That's because AI agents, powered by the bleeding-edge foundation models developed by companies like Meta and OpenAI, still can't reliably take actions across the web, particularly those involving phone calls. Former Yahoo CEO Marissa Mayer, who now helms agent startup Dazzle AI, says current top-tier AI models excel at surfacing online home renovation services for consumers, but might blow it when they need to book and schedule a rooftop upgrade."We're relying on the frontier models to give us good suggestions and a good candidate list, but we're checking that over to make sure that we're really delivering the type of service that we can stand behind," Mayer said, referring to how Dazzle funnels certain tasks to human contractors.Digital assistants driven by artificial intelligence are currently gaining renewed interest thanks to Meta, OpenAI and others that are pitching the technology as capable of tasks like scouting the internet for shoes.Meta's Muse, OpenAI's Dots and a host of other agents can accomplish a multitude of web-browsing feats, but it's still early days for the technology, and it often hits digital roadblocks. Those barriers typically involve tasks that would have an AI agent make a phone call, schedule a doctor's appointment on someone's behalf, or reserve a couch scrubbing from a local cleaning service, said Meghan Joyce, CEO of digital agent startup Duckbill.For tasks that require real-world judgment, Joyce said humans still trump AI, and companies building consumer-grade digital assistants will need to patch in real people to take over. That's why Duckbill recently debuted an application programming interface, or API, intended for companies building personal agents to connect with human contract workers."We work on a model that is not dissimilar from Uber, where we boil tasks down into atomic bite-sized pieces," Joyce said, referencing the ride-hailing company where she previously worked.Companies making agents can use Duckbill's API to delegate the tasks that the agent is likely to fumble. Duckbill translates those tasks into bite-sized pieces that the average adult can do consistently and reliably. "And then we track what happens," Joyce said. Confused agentsMayer said that AI models can still lack common sense. She said a Dazzle AI super user attempted to have the technology simultaneously handle a series of home renovation projects involving a roof replacement, a broken window and the purchase of a glass tabletop.But the AI agent, Mayer said, confused window glass with tabletop glass, resulting in the digital assistant "trying to figure out if he could make the tabletop fit in the window."The mishap didn't last long, Mayer said, because Dazzle's technology flagged the task and outsourced it to a person to complete."Within a few seconds, the human had things sorted out. Whereas an agent would have burned a ridiculous number of tokens," Mayer said. "Or they may never have gotten to a good solution."Shivani Poddar, CEO of personal AI agent startup Wajo AI, is also incorporating human workers to handle phone calls and even CAPTCHA tests intended to fend off bots from sites."I think AI plus humans, collaborative AI, is what you need to actually get the job done," Poddar said, emphasizing that people will stop using the technology if agents can't complete tasks. watch nowChatbot and agent interactions can be ultra personal and users have good reason to be concerned about the humans stepping in, particularly if the company didn't tell them how it works. Meta employees previously raised privacy concerns about the company's internal test using human contractors to handle phone calls on behalf of its Muse AI agent. A Meta spokesperson said in a statement at the time that this kind of testing is "core to the product development process."Meta currently doesn't use humans to complete users' Muse requests.Duckbill's Joyce said her startup does "full background checking" into the 1099 contractors it uses, comparing them to drivers for Uber and DoorDash, "people who live here in the United States and want a source of additional income." Duckbill also uses contract workers from businesses that typically offer contact center labor to companies.Mayer said Dazzle conducts background checks and looks for contractors with the same qualities someone might look for in a human personal assistant. "We generally are screening for people who we think are extremely discreet and have good taste and good judgment, both in terms of how they interact with our users, but just the ability to kind of forget and compartmentalize that information afterwards," Mayer said. "I understand it's a point of privilege, but I've had personal assistants for some time, and I know how I want them, and I know how I guide them."Mayer said that while foundation models are still improving, the market is in a "transitionary period" until the technology can perform more involved web tasks and phone calls as efficiently as people."We're not even trying to hide it, we think the human in the loop is a benefit," Mayer said.WATCH: Who's liable when AI agents break the rules?watch now

schema.headline: Humans are still doing the work behind some AI agents

title: ‘Pop-up’ super PACs pour $637 million into 2026 midterm races
description: watch nowA super PAC called Our Heritage Matters registered with the Federal Election Commission on Oct. 15.Five days later, it began spending to boos
body: watch nowA super PAC called Our Heritage Matters registered with the Federal Election Commission on Oct. 15.Five days later, it began spending to boost third-party candidates and attack Republicans. By Oct. 29, the group had spent about $1.2 million across 10 House and Senate races, according to a CNBC analysis of FEC filings.What voters still cannot see is who supplied the money.Because Our Heritage Matters formed after a key campaign finance reporting deadline on Oct. 15, its first regular report identifying its donors is not due until Dec. 3, a month after Election Day.The group is an extreme example of a broader surge reshaping the midterm election: late-forming super PACs, including the latest-forming "pop-up PACs," pouring money into races before voters know where it came from.Federal law requires super PACs and political committees to report large independent expenditures within 24 or 48 hours depending on how close to Election Day the spending occurs, showing how much they spent and which candidates they supported or opposed. Their donors, however, are disclosed less frequently through periodic campaign finance reports.And in 2026, the practice of creating new, last-minute PACs has exploded. Both parties are using the tactic, with Republican-linked PACs spending about twice what those connected with Democrats have disbursed.Twenty-two super PACs that registered with the FEC during the final 10 weeks before Election Day have each spent at least $1 million on congressional races, according to CNBC's analysis. Together, they had reported roughly $637 million in independent expenditures by Oct. 29 — about one-sixth of all independent spending reported in House and Senate races this election cycle. The number of million-dollar late-forming super PACs has more than quadrupled since 2022, while their spending has grown nearly 35-fold.At the same point in the 2022 midterms, just five comparable groups had spent about $18 million combined, according to CNBC's analysis. In 2018, three had spent about $12 million. The total has even eclipsed the past two presidential elections, when comparable late-forming super PACs spent less than $50 million combined on congressional races in both 2020 and 2024, according to CNBC's analysis."The reason for this is almost entirely to avoid disclosure, even if just temporarily," said Michael Kang, a Northwestern Pritzker School of Law professor who studies campaign finance. "Many times, if the donors were known, then it would undercut their cause."CNBC's analysis includes super PACs formed in the final 10 weeks before Election Day that spent at least $1 million on House or Senate races by Oct. 29. Spending includes regular FEC filings and 24- and 48-hour reports, with duplicates removed. From zero to millions in late-forming PAC spendingOne of the defining features of late-forming super PACs is speed.Among the 22 groups in CNBC's analysis, 18 began spending within 30 days of launching, and almost all started spending before filing their first regular campaign finance report showing where their money came from.“It’s happening more often, and they’re spending more money doing it because it works, and they’re getting away with it,” said Saurav Ghosh, director of federal campaign finance reform at the Campaign Legal Center. The group is a nonpartisan nonprofit founded by a former Republican FEC chairman.Despite their late start, the groups accounted for more than 22% of independent expenditures in congressional races during CNBC's 2026 window, up from less than 2% at the same point in each of the previous two midterms.Many are new only on paper. CNBC found financial or organizational ties between nine of the 22 groups and established political networks.Lower Costs Now, for example, formed on Sept. 10 and disclosed an affiliation with the Future Forward PAC, the main outside group that backed former Vice President Kamala Harris' 2024 presidential campaign. Nineteen days later, Lower Costs Now began spending in Senate races.But voters did not get a fuller picture of its financing until Oct. 15, when its first regular financial report showed that Senate Majority PAC, the main super PAC working to elect Senate Democrats, had given the group $23 million, according to FEC filings.By Thursday, Lower Costs Now had reported about $75.5 million in independent expenditures across eight Senate contests, including Iowa, Texas, Kansas and Ohio, according to CNBC's analysis.Republicans have used the same playbook.No Going Back PAC formed Sept. 1 and began spending three days later. Public reporting soon linked it to MAGA Inc., President Donald Trump's marquee super PAC. But its formal financial report did not arrive until Oct. 20 — more than six weeks after the spending began.By then, No Going Back had already spent roughly $187.8 million, according to FEC filings, which revealed that MAGA Inc. had supplied the group with $200 million. By Thursday, the super PAC had spent roughly $242.2 million, according to FEC filings.“They are a vehicle designed to emerge from nowhere and spend a bunch of money on an election” before voters can learn “who’s supplying that money and what their motivations might be,” Ghosh said.PACs built for one race Many of the new groups are also narrowly targeted.Fourteen of the 22 million-dollar super PACs identified by CNBC spent all of their money in a single congressional contest.Take The Maine Standard. It formed Sept. 11 and began spending five days later. Since then, it has spent $8.2 million, all of it opposing Democrat Troy Jackson in Maine's Senate race, according to FEC filings.The Cornhusker Majority followed almost the same pattern. It formed Sept. 10, began spending Sept. 16 and has spent about $7.1 million in Nebraska's Senate race, almost all of it opposing independent Dan Osborn, according to FEC filings. Osborn is running against Republican incumbent Sen. Pete Ricketts in a tight race.The connection between the two groups did not appear in their regular financial reports until Oct. 15: Both were financed by Senate Leadership Fund, the GOP's main Senate super PAC.On the Democratic side, Texas Forever launched Sept. 24 and began spending five days later, according to FEC filings. By Thursday, it had spent about $27.5 million to help Democratic Texas Senate nominee James Talarico, according to the FEC. Unlike some other pop-up groups, however, its initial FEC filing identified the Senate Majority PAC as an affiliate."A locally branded PAC doesn't necessarily hide where the money comes from, but it fragments the picture. Instead of seeing one national organization spending tens of millions of dollars across the country, voters see a series of different groups operating race by race," said Hilary Braseth, executive director of OpenSecrets, a nonpartisan nonprofit that tracks such spending.But even identifying the national group behind a pop-up PAC can still leave another layer of the money trail hidden.Texas PAC formed Aug. 28 and soon began spending to help Republican Ken Paxton in Texas' Senate race. The money flowed through the SLF, but Elon Musk's role was not public until Oct. 12, more than a month after the spending began.On Oct. 15, FEC filings showed Musk had given the SLF $158 million in two contributions, with the group transferring matching amounts to Texas PAC the day after each donation.By Oct. 29, Texas PAC had spent about $181.6 million in the race, according to FEC filings, making it one of the largest late-forming super PACs CNBC identified.Together, Texas PAC and No Going Back accounted for roughly two-thirds of all spending by the 22 million-dollar groups. But the surge was much broader than those two giants: Even excluding them, the remaining groups spent nearly 12 times as much as comparable late-forming super PACs did at the same point in 2022."The growth is huge this year," Kang said. "Maybe you don’t want to be known this election, or want to hide away for a period while you might be unpopular, like AI is right now, but you kind of want to build a reputation for the players inside the system."

schema.headline: ‘Pop-up’ super PACs pour $637 million into 2026 midterm races

title: Automakers like Rivian and Ford are ‘democratizing 3D printing’ to reduce costs and increase speed

body: watch nowDETROIT — Automakers including Ford Motor and Rivian Automotive are leaning into a new type of manufacturing line: 3D printing.Manufacturers say it's helping them reduce costs and increase speed. The technology has been around for decades, but it's becoming more commoditized in the automotive industry, with 3D printers used to create everything from vehicle parts and accessories to tools for assembly plants and testing units for research and development labs."At this point, we don't have a choice but to scale up and begin using it through all factions of Rivian," Jared Beck, head of Rivian's additive manufacturing, told CNBC during a tour of the automaker's expansive 3D-printing operations in suburban Detroit. "We're going to be democratizing 3D printing for the entire company."The benefits of 3D printingAlso known as additive manufacturing, 3D printing can create three-dimensional objects from digital designs by dispensing material layer by layer, much like a traditional printer does with ink on paper. Instead of ink, the machines use a wide variety of materials such as plastics, composites, ceramics and even metals.The progression of the new steering wheel for Rivian's new R2 SUV from 3D print to finished design for production at its facility in Plymouth, Michigan.Michael Wayland / CNBCPrinters can range from hundreds of dollars for hobby-like devices to hundreds of thousands of dollars for specialty equipment, depending on how big the product being produced is and the material it needs. They can produce individual pieces or hundreds of smaller parts in a batch using powders and resins.Rivian said it has spent more than $5 million on 3D-printing machines, with the cost of materials for the operations growing to about $1.7 million annually.Beck said despite the costs, the machines typically pay for themselves within a year. He said the technology helps lower supplier tooling costs, streamline logistics expenses and cut production times for parts from weeks to days, if not hours."It's well in the millions [for savings], but the main thing is speed for Rivian," Beck said. The all-electric vehicle company's latest expansion of 3D printing includes adding new machines that can build flexible silicone parts as well as installing a bay of machines at its plant in Normal, Illinois, for employees to print parts on demand.A 3D-printed version of Rivian's cartoon Yeti mascot named Gary stands inside an additive manufacturing area at Rivian's facility in Plymouth, Michigan.Michael Wayland / CNBC"3D prints should be readily available for every engineer so that they can make a part and get it in their hands as soon as possible," Beck said.Rivian has also used the technology for electric-motor models for fluid testing, creating screw guides for tooling and stamping press inserts and some production parts, including trim pieces to fill gaps in some early builds.GM, FordThere's a similar push underway at larger, more-established automakers like Ford and its crosstown rival General Motors, which have used 3D printing for many years, including in their massive assembly plants.Instead of having a bay of 3D-printing machines like at Rivian, Ford has departments for additive manufacturing at many of its plants to produce and distribute needed parts. That includes a new vending machine for 3D-printed parts for production of F-150 pickup trucks near its Dearborn, Michigan, headquarters.Gregory Foresi, a Ford mechanical engineer, holds up a device he 3D printed to reinstall vehicle badges onto the automaker's F-150 pickup trucks inside the River Rouge factory in Dearborn, Michigan. Michael Wayland / CNBC "By putting the vending machine up, all the team leaders have access," said Gregory Foresi, a Ford mechanical engineer who ran Ford's 3D-printing lab at the plant from 2024 until last month. "We're able to keep that thing stocked rather than have a bunch of parts laying around in the lab. So that's been pretty huge."Foresi used roughly two dozen machines to print off thousands of tools, some of which have been designed by employees, such as torque bit sockets, hood jackers and hand tools for smoothing adhesive.Employees can use an app to request that specific auto parts or tools be printed. Ford's 3D-printing teams help develop them or determine what to produce next, as the machining time to build different parts can range from hours to days, if not weeks.Foresi said creating the tools with 3D printing has allowed the automaker to uniquely design them when needed, get them faster and, in many cases, receive them at a lower cost. Ford also has used 3D-printed parts to help keep production running. For example, Foresi said a large machining wheel was needed to maintain assembly line production and the company was able to 3D print the part until a permanent replacement from a supplier was available.A table full of 3D-printed parts and tools inside the 3D-printing lab at Ford's River Rouge factory in Dearborn, Michigan.Michael Wayland / CNBC"They didn't perform as well, and it's not really a replacement for the ones that we were purchasing, but they kept the plant running," Foresi said.Ford said it expects to have 3D labs deployed at more than 23 plants by the end of this year. Its current 3D-printing program has more than 200 machines, and there are additional printers outside the official program, the company said.GM has used 3D-printed parts for some of its low-volume products in addition to research and development and inside plants, including recently expanding its use of industrial Stratasys printers that can cost hundreds of thousands of dollars based on use case, training and certification.The Detroit automaker uses 135 components that are 3D-printed for its bespoke Cadillac Celestiq as well as other components for its performance Cadillac Blackwing sedans, including a unique medallion on the manual shifter knob.Fadi Abro, senior global director of automotive and mobility at 3D-printing company Stratasys, said GM has been a great example of how companies can "standardize and then scale" 3D printing. "The material properties improved so significantly that the use cases improved," he said, noting the company works with virtually every major automaker. "From a product perspective, we have to get the technology to become faster and more accessible, in an economic sense."A GM metal model maker wipes dust from a 3D printer in between part builds at one of the Detroit automaker's facilities.Courtesy GM

schema.headline: Automakers like Rivian and Ford are ‘democratizing 3D printing’ to reduce costs and increase speed
